Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 97, verses 1–3:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Aisha, when she asked him what she should supplicate with if she happened upon the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr):

"Say: O Allah, You are Pardoning (ʿAfuww) and You love pardon, so pardon me."

(Sahih)

And he (ﷺ) said, similar to this:

"Whoever stands (in prayer) on the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking reward, his past sins will be forgiven."

(A subtle point worth drawing attention to)

It is that Abu Dharr asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Night of Decree and pressed him insistently, until the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him at the end of his question: "Seek it in the last ten nights, and do not ask me about anything after this." Then he (ﷺ) spoke and talked at length. Abu Dharr said: "I seized his moment of distraction and said: 'I adjure you, O Messenger of Allah, by my right over you, to tell me which of the ten nights it is.' He became angry with me, a anger he had never shown me before or after. Then he said: 'Seek it in the last seven nights, and do not ask me about anything further.'"

And in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in he said:

"He (ﷺ) was asked about the Night of Decree: is it in Ramadan or in another month? He said: 'Rather, it is in Ramadan.' It was said: 'Will it remain with the Prophets as long as they are alive, and when they die will it be lifted, or will it remain until the Day of Resurrection?' He said: 'Rather, it will remain until the Day of Resurrection.' It was said: 'In which Ramadan is it?' He said: 'Seek it in the first ten nights, or in the last ten nights.' It was said: 'In which of the twenty?' He said: 'Seek it in the last ten nights, and do not ask me about anything after it.' He said: 'I adjure you by my right over you, to tell me which of the ten nights it is.' He became very angry and said: 'Seek it in the last seven nights, and do not ask me anything further about it.'" Ahmad mentioned this, and the questioner was Abu Dharr. In Abu Dawud's collection: "He (ﷺ) was asked about the Night of Decree and said: 'It is in every Ramadan.'"

"He was also asked about it, and said: 'How many nights remain?' The questioner said: 'Twenty-two.' He said: 'It is this night'; then he reconsidered and said: 'Or the next,' meaning the twenty-third." Abu Dawud mentioned this.

Abdullah ibn Unays asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "When should we seek this blessed night?" He said: "Seek it this night, which is the evening of the twenty-third night."

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) asked him (ﷺ): "If I happen upon it, what should I supplicate with?" He said: "Say: O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me."

A sahih hadith.

(Benefit)

This is the statement of one who said that the Night of Decree has been lifted.

If this person means that its knowledge was known and then its knowledge was lifted from the Ummah, it is said to him: its knowledge was not lifted from the entire Ummah, even if it was lifted from some of them. If he means that its reality and its being an hour of answered supplication was lifted, then this is a false statement that contradicts the sound and explicit hadiths, so it should not be relied upon. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Shu'ba narrated from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. He said: "It is the child." This was also said by al-Hakam, Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

The strongest report on this is what Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated from his father, who said: "My uncle narrated to me, my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas," who said: "It is the child." Ibn Zayd said: "It is intercourse." Qatada said: "Seek the concession which Allah has prescribed for you." And there is another report from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is the Night of Decree."

The verification is to say: when Allah lightened the burden on the Ummah by permitting intercourse during the nights of fasting until the break of dawn, and the one who engages in intercourse is usually overcome by desire and the fulfilment of need, to the point that hardly anything else comes to his heart, Allah (Glorified is He) guided them to seek His pleasure even in this pleasure. They should not engage in it merely under the sway of desire, but rather seek through it what Allah has prescribed for them: the reward, and the child who will come forth from their loins and worship Allah, associating nothing with Him. They should also seek what Allah has permitted them as a concession, out of His love for His concessions being accepted, for Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He dislikes that His disobedience be committed. Among what He has prescribed for them is the Night of Decree, and they were commanded to seek it. But there remains the question: what is the connection of that with the permission of relations with their wives? It is said: there is in it guidance that the permission they have for relations should not distract them from seeking this night, which is better than a thousand months. It is as if He (Glorified is He) says: fulfil your needs with your wives during the nights of fasting, but let that not distract you from seeking what Allah has prescribed for you in this night, with which Allah has favoured you. And Allah knows best.

(Question)

If you ask: which of the two tens is better, the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, or the last ten nights of Ramadan?

And which of the two nights is better, the Night of Decree, or the Night of the Isra' (Night Journey)?

I say: as for the first question, the correct answer is: the nights of the last ten of Ramadan are better than the nights of the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the days of the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah are better than the days of the ten of Ramadan. With this distinction the confusion disappears. This is indicated by the fact that the nights of the ten of Ramadan are only preferred because of the Night of Decree, which is among the nights, whereas the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah is preferred because of its days, since in it are the Day of Sacrifice, the Day of ʿArafah, and the Day of Tarwiyah.

As for the second question, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) was asked about a man who said: "The Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree." Another said: "Rather, the Night of Decree is better. Which of them is correct?"

He answered: "All praise is due to Allah. As for the one who says the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree: if he means that the night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, and its counterparts every year, are better for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) than the Night of Decree, such that standing in prayer and supplicating in it is more excellent than in the Night of Decree, then this is false. No one among the Muslims has said it, and it is known to be corrupt by the consistent practice of the religion of Islam.

This is so even if the Night of the Isra' were known in its specific identity. How much more so when there is no known evidence either for its month, its ten, or its exact night. Rather, the reports about it are disconnected and contradictory, and there is nothing in them that can be relied upon with certainty. It is not legislated for Muslims to single out the night that is supposed to be the Night of the Isra' with night prayer or anything else. This differs from the Night of Decree, for it is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Seek the Night of Decree in the last ten nights of Ramadan.' And in the two Sahihs from him (ﷺ) that he said: 'Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking reward, his past sins will be forgiven.' Allah (Glorified is He) has informed us that it is better than a thousand months, and that He sent down the Qur'an in it.

If he means that the specific night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, and in which he received what he had not received in any other night, without it being legislated to single it out with night prayer or worship, then this is correct. But it does not follow that when Allah grants His Prophet (ﷺ) a virtue in a place or a time, that time and place must be better than all places and times.

This is the case if it were established that Allah's favour upon His Prophet (ﷺ) on the Night of the Isra' was greater than His favour upon him through the sending down of the Qur'an on the Night of Decree, and other blessings with which He favoured him.

Discussion of such matters requires knowledge of the realities of affairs and the measures of blessings, which are not known except through revelation. No one may speak about them without knowledge. Nor is it known of any of the Muslims that he made the Night of the Isra' more virtuous than other nights, especially than the Night of Decree. Nor did the Companions and those who followed them in excellence intend to single out the Night of the Isra' with any matter or mention it. For this reason, it is not known which night it was, although the Isra' is among the greatest of his (ﷺ) virtues. And despite this, it was not legislated to single out that time or that place for a legislated act of worship. Rather, the Cave of Hira, where the revelation began and where he used to seclude himself before prophethood, was not targeted by him or by any of his Companions after prophethood during his stay in Makkah. Nor was the day on which the revelation was sent down singled out for worship or anything else, nor was the place where revelation began, nor the time, singled out for anything. Whoever singles out places and times for acts of worship on his own authority, for this reason and similar ones, is of the same kind as the People of the Book who made the times of the events of the Messiah into festivals and acts of worship, such as the Day of Birth, the Day of Baptism, and other events of his life."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) saw a group rushing toward a place to pray in it. He said: "What is this?" They said: "A place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed." He said: "Do you want to take the traces of your prophets as places of worship? Those before you were destroyed only by this. Whoever is overtaken by the prayer in it should pray, and otherwise let him pass on."

Some people have said: the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree with regard to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the Night of Decree is better with regard to the Ummah. So this night is better for them, and the Night of the Isra' is better for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If it is said: which is better, Friday or the Day of ʿArafah? Ibn Hibban narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The sun does not rise or set on a day better than Friday." And in the same collection is the hadith of Aws ibn Aws: "The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday."

(Benefit)

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to observe i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) in the last ten nights of Ramadan until Allah took him (Mighty and Majestic is He). Once he left it, and then made it up in Shawwal.

He once observed i'tikaf in the first ten, then the middle ten, then the last ten, seeking the Night of Decree. Then it became clear to him that it was in the last ten, so he persisted in his i'tikaf until he met his Lord (Mighty and Majestic is He).

He used to order a tent to be pitched for him in the mosque, where he would be alone with his Lord (Mighty and Majestic is He).

(Section: on mentioning the fourth estimate, the Night of Decree)

Allah (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Ha-Mim. By the Clear Book. Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night. Indeed, We were ever warning. In it is made distinct every wise matter, by command from Us. Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 1–5]. This is the Night of Decree, definitively, based on His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

Whoever claims that it is the night of the middle of Sha'ban has erred.

Sufyan narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The Night of Decree is the Night of Judgment." Sufyan also narrated from Muhammad ibn Suqah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Permission is given to the pilgrims during the Night of Decree, and they are registered by their names and their fathers' names, so not one of them is left out, nor is anything added to them or subtracted from them." Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us from Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum, who said: A man said to al-Hasan, while I was listening: "Do you think the Night of Decree occurs in every Ramadan?" He said: "Yes, by Allah, other than whom there is no god, it is in every Ramadan, and it is indeed the Night of Decree, in which every wise matter is made distinct. In it Allah decides every term, deed, and provision until the next one like it."

Yusuf ibn Mihran mentioned from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Night of Decree, what will happen in the year is written down from the Mother of the Book: death, life, provision, and rain, even the pilgrims. It is said: so-and-so will perform Hajj, and so-and-so will perform Hajj."

It was mentioned from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding this verse: "You will see a man walking in the markets while his name has been entered among the dead."

Muqatil said: "In the Night of Decree, Allah decrees the affairs of the year regarding His lands and servants until the following year."

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: "He decrees the affairs of the entire year in the Night of Decree."

This is the correct view: qadr is the verbal noun of "qadara al-shay'" (he measured/decreed the thing), so it is the Night of Judgment and Decree.

A group said: the Night of Decree is the Night of Honour and Greatness, from the expression "li-fulan qadr fi al-nas" (so-and-so has standing among people). If the one who holds this view means that it has a standing and honour together with what is decreed in it, he is correct. And in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in he said:

"He (ﷺ) was asked about the Night of Decree: is it in Ramadan or in another month? He said: 'Rather, it is in Ramadan.' It was said: 'Will it remain with the Prophets as long as they are alive, and when they die will it be lifted, or will it remain until the Day of Resurrection?' He said: 'Rather, it will remain until the Day of Resurrection.' It was said: 'In which Ramadan is it?' He said: 'Seek it in the first ten nights, or in the last ten nights.' It was said: 'In which of the twenty?' He said: 'Seek it in the last ten nights, and do not ask me about anything after it.' He said: 'I adjure you by my right over you, to tell me which of the ten nights it is.' He became very angry and said: 'Seek it in the last seven nights, and do not ask me anything further about it.'" Ahmad mentioned this, and the questioner was Abu Dharr. In Abu Dawud's collection: "He (ﷺ) was asked about the Night of Decree and said: 'It is in every Ramadan.'"

"He was also asked about it, and said: 'How many nights remain?' The questioner said: 'Twenty-two.' He said: 'It is this night'; then he reconsidered and said: 'Or the next,' meaning the twenty-third." Abu Dawud mentioned this.

Abdullah ibn Unays asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "When should we seek this blessed night?" He said: "Seek it this night, which is the evening of the twenty-third night."

Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) asked him (ﷺ): "If I happen upon it, what should I supplicate with?" He said: "Say: O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me."

A sahih hadith.

(Benefit)

This is the statement of one who said that the Night of Decree has been lifted.

If this person means that its knowledge was known and then its knowledge was lifted from the Ummah, it is said to him: its knowledge was not lifted from the entire Ummah, even if it was lifted from some of them. If he means that its reality and its being an hour of answered supplication was lifted, then this is a false statement that contradicts the sound and explicit hadiths, so it should not be relied upon. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

Shu'ba narrated from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. He said: "It is the child." This was also said by al-Hakam, Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

The strongest report on this is what Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated from his father, who said: "My uncle narrated to me, my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas," who said: "It is the child." Ibn Zayd said: "It is intercourse." Qatada said: "Seek the concession which Allah has prescribed for you." And there is another report from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It is the Night of Decree."

The verification is to say: when Allah lightened the burden on the Ummah by permitting intercourse during the nights of fasting until the break of dawn, and the one who engages in intercourse is usually overcome by desire and the fulfilment of need, to the point that hardly anything else comes to his heart, Allah (Glorified is He) guided them to seek His pleasure even in this pleasure. They should not engage in it merely under the sway of desire, but rather seek through it what Allah has prescribed for them: the reward, and the child who will come forth from their loins and worship Allah, associating nothing with Him. They should also seek what Allah has permitted them as a concession, out of His love for His concessions being accepted, for Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He dislikes that His disobedience be committed. Among what He has prescribed for them is the Night of Decree, and they were commanded to seek it. But there remains the question: what is the connection of that with the permission of relations with their wives? It is said: there is in it guidance that the permission they have for relations should not distract them from seeking this night, which is better than a thousand months. It is as if He (Glorified is He) says: fulfil your needs with your wives during the nights of fasting, but let that not distract you from seeking what Allah has prescribed for you in this night, with which Allah has favoured you. And Allah knows best.

(Question)

If you ask: which of the two tens is better, the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, or the last ten nights of Ramadan?

And which of the two nights is better, the Night of Decree, or the Night of the Isra' (Night Journey)?

I say: as for the first question, the correct answer is: the nights of the last ten of Ramadan are better than the nights of the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the days of the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah are better than the days of the ten of Ramadan. With this distinction the confusion disappears. This is indicated by the fact that the nights of the ten of Ramadan are only preferred because of the Night of Decree, which is among the nights, whereas the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah is preferred because of its days, since in it are the Day of Sacrifice, the Day of ʿArafah, and the Day of Tarwiyah.

As for the second question, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) was asked about a man who said: "The Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree." Another said: "Rather, the Night of Decree is better. Which of them is correct?"

He answered: "All praise is due to Allah. As for the one who says the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree: if he means that the night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, and its counterparts every year, are better for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) than the Night of Decree, such that standing in prayer and supplicating in it is more excellent than in the Night of Decree, then this is false. No one among the Muslims has said it, and it is known to be corrupt by the consistent practice of the religion of Islam.

This is so even if the Night of the Isra' were known in its specific identity. How much more so when there is no known evidence either for its month, its ten, or its exact night. Rather, the reports about it are disconnected and contradictory, and there is nothing in them that can be relied upon with certainty. It is not legislated for Muslims to single out the night that is supposed to be the Night of the Isra' with night prayer or anything else. This differs from the Night of Decree, for it is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Seek the Night of Decree in the last ten nights of Ramadan.' And in the two Sahihs from him (ﷺ) that he said: 'Whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Decree out of faith and seeking reward, his past sins will be forgiven.' Allah (Glorified is He) has informed us that it is better than a thousand months, and that He sent down the Qur'an in it.

If he means that the specific night in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, and in which he received what he had not received in any other night, without it being legislated to single it out with night prayer or worship, then this is correct. But it does not follow that when Allah grants His Prophet (ﷺ) a virtue in a place or a time, that time and place must be better than all places and times.

This is the case if it were established that Allah's favour upon His Prophet (ﷺ) on the Night of the Isra' was greater than His favour upon him through the sending down of the Qur'an on the Night of Decree, and other blessings with which He favoured him.

Discussion of such matters requires knowledge of the realities of affairs and the measures of blessings, which are not known except through revelation. No one may speak about them without knowledge. Nor is it known of any of the Muslims that he made the Night of the Isra' more virtuous than other nights, especially than the Night of Decree. Nor did the Companions and those who followed them in excellence intend to single out the Night of the Isra' with any matter or mention it. For this reason, it is not known which night it was, although the Isra' is among the greatest of his (ﷺ) virtues. And despite this, it was not legislated to single out that time or that place for a legislated act of worship. Rather, the Cave of Hira, where the revelation began and where he used to seclude himself before prophethood, was not targeted by him or by any of his Companions after prophethood during his stay in Makkah. Nor was the day on which the revelation was sent down singled out for worship or anything else, nor was the place where revelation began, nor the time, singled out for anything. Whoever singles out places and times for acts of worship on his own authority, for this reason and similar ones, is of the same kind as the People of the Book who made the times of the events of the Messiah into festivals and acts of worship, such as the Day of Birth, the Day of Baptism, and other events of his life."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) saw a group rushing toward a place to pray in it. He said: "What is this?" They said: "A place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed." He said: "Do you want to take the traces of your prophets as places of worship? Those before you were destroyed only by this. Whoever is overtaken by the prayer in it should pray, and otherwise let him pass on."

Some people have said: the Night of the Isra' is better than the Night of Decree with regard to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the Night of Decree is better with regard to the Ummah. So this night is better for them, and the Night of the Isra' is better for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

If it is said: which is better, Friday or the Day of ʿArafah? Ibn Hibban narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The sun does not rise or set on a day better than Friday." And in the same collection is the hadith of Aws ibn Aws: "The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday."

(Benefit)

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to observe i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque) in the last ten nights of Ramadan until Allah took him (Mighty and Majestic is He). Once he left it, and then made it up in Shawwal.

He once observed i'tikaf in the first ten, then the middle ten, then the last ten, seeking the Night of Decree. Then it became clear to him that it was in the last ten, so he persisted in his i'tikaf until he met his Lord (Mighty and Majestic is He).

He used to order a tent to be pitched for him in the mosque, where he would be alone with his Lord (Mighty and Majestic is He).

(Section: on mentioning the fourth estimate, the Night of Decree)

Allah (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Ha-Mim. By the Clear Book. Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night. Indeed, We were ever warning. In it is made distinct every wise matter, by command from Us. Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 1–5]. This is the Night of Decree, definitively, based on His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

Whoever claims that it is the night of the middle of Sha'ban has erred.

Sufyan narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "The Night of Decree is the Night of Judgment." Sufyan also narrated from Muhammad ibn Suqah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Permission is given to the pilgrims during the Night of Decree, and they are registered by their names and their fathers' names, so not one of them is left out, nor is anything added to them or subtracted from them." Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us from Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum, who said: A man said to al-Hasan, while I was listening: "Do you think the Night of Decree occurs in every Ramadan?" He said: "Yes, by Allah, other than whom there is no god, it is in every Ramadan, and it is indeed the Night of Decree, in which every wise matter is made distinct. In it Allah decides every term, deed, and provision until the next one like it."

Yusuf ibn Mihran mentioned from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Night of Decree, what will happen in the year is written down from the Mother of the Book: death, life, provision, and rain, even the pilgrims. It is said: so-and-so will perform Hajj, and so-and-so will perform Hajj."

It was mentioned from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding this verse: "You will see a man walking in the markets while his name has been entered among the dead."

Muqatil said: "In the Night of Decree, Allah decrees the affairs of the year regarding His lands and servants until the following year."

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: "He decrees the affairs of the entire year in the Night of Decree."

This is the correct view: qadr is the verbal noun of "qadara al-shay'" (he measured/decreed the thing), so it is the Night of Judgment and Decree.

A group said: the Night of Decree is the Night of Honour and Greatness, from the expression "li-fulan qadr fi al-nas" (so-and-so has standing among people). If the one who holds this view means that it has a standing and honour together with what is decreed in it, he is correct. But if he means that the meaning of qadr in it is honour and eminence, then he has erred, for Allah (Glorified is He) has informed us that in it "every wise matter is made distinct," that is, Allah makes clear, explains, and firmly decides every wise matter.
